client: Lately I've been really struggling at work since my dad passed. I'll just be sitting at my desk trying to focus, and then suddenly I'm either tearing up or just filled with this angry frustration that he's gone. It's making me mess up simple tasks, and I'm worried my coworkers are noticing. To be honest, I'm not even sure talking about it will help - the grief just feels too heavy.
therapist:
I hear how deeply painful and disruptive this grief has been for you at work. What stands out is that even when you say talking might not help, you're still reaching out - that takes courage when the weight feels so heavy. 

Would it be okay to explore how these sudden waves of anger and sadness show up in your body when they come at work?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess it starts with this tightness in my chest, like I can't breathe properly. Then my hands get shaky and I have to clench them under my desk. But I don't know how noticing that helps - the feelings just crash over me anyway.
therapist: It sounds like these moments bring such intense physical reactions - that tightness and shakiness must feel overwhelming. I'm noticing you're describing this very vividly even while doubting whether noticing helps, which makes me curious: what happens right before you first notice that tightness in your chest?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: Sometimes it's nothing obvious - I'll just see the date on my computer or hear someone mention their dad. Other times I'll be working on something he taught me, like these spreadsheets... but I don't want to avoid my work just because it reminds me of him. That feels like losing him all over again.
therapist:
What a meaningful way to honor your dad - pushing through the pain to keep engaging with what he taught you. That tightness seems to show up in those moments when memories unexpectedly connect your present to your loss. 

Would it feel okay to experiment with something? Next time you notice that chest tightness while working on spreadsheets, could you try pausing just for a breath to acknowledge "This is me missing dad" before continuing?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess I could try that, but I'm worried it might make things worse. What if acknowledging it just makes me cry at my desk? I'm already barely holding it together as it is. But... I do like the idea of honoring him by continuing his lessons. That feels right somehow.
therapist:
I hear your concern about acknowledging the grief potentially making things harder at work - that's a very valid worry when you're already feeling so raw. What strikes me is how strongly your voice conveys both the struggle and the heartfelt connection to honoring your dad's memory. 

Would it help to think of these moments not as breaking down, but as brief pauses to honor what he meant to you? Even if tears come, they might be part of that honoring.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: I never thought of it that way - as honoring him instead of breaking down. But I'm still worried about crying at work. What if someone sees? I don't want to be the person everyone has to tiptoe around or feel sorry for. Maybe I could try this pausing thing when I'm alone in my office though. That feels a little safer.
therapist:
It sounds like you're finding a thoughtful balance between honoring your grief and maintaining your professional environment. Starting with private moments in your office feels like a compassionate way to ease into this new approach. 

What would it feel like to think of those private pauses as a safe space to reconnect with your dad's memory, even if just for a breath?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: It does feel comforting to think of those moments as safe spaces rather than something to avoid. But I worry I'll still feel overwhelmed - like I'm opening a floodgate I can't close. What if I can't stop crying once I start? I guess I'm scared of losing control entirely.
therapist:
Your fear about opening a floodgate makes complete sense - grief can feel so unpredictable and powerful. I notice you're describing this with such care while also being willing to consider this approach, which shows real strength. 

What if we thought about these pauses not as opening floodgates, but as brief moments of connection that you can choose to end when needed? You're still in control here.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: That actually helps to think of it that way - like I'm choosing to connect with him rather than being ambushed by grief. But how do I really know I can stop when I want to? Yesterday I saw his favorite candy in the store and had to leave because I couldn't stop crying in the checkout line. It's not always that simple.
therapist: It sounds like that candy store moment really shook your confidence in being able to manage these waves of grief - no wonder you're cautious. What I'm hearing is that some situations feel more overwhelming than others, which makes me curious about how that checkout line moment was different from when you're at your desk?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: At the store, it was so public and unexpected - I couldn't prepare myself at all. At my desk, at least I can see when I'm about to work on something he taught me. But honestly, I'm not sure preparation even helps - grief still hits me like a truck either way. Maybe I just have to accept that some days will be worse than others.
therapist:
You're making such an important observation here - that grief has its own unpredictable rhythm, with some days hitting harder than others. I notice your voice carries more intensity when you describe these sudden waves, even as your words acknowledge the need for acceptance. 

This makes me wonder - what would it feel like to approach these harder moments with the same understanding you're showing now, rather than fighting them?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: That's hard to imagine - approaching the pain instead of fighting it. But I guess fighting hasn't really helped so far either. It's just... accepting it feels like giving up somehow, like I'm letting the grief win. I don't want to stop missing him, but I don't want to be consumed by it either.
therapist:
You're touching on something really profound here - that tension between fearing acceptance means surrender while recognizing that resistance hasn't helped either. There's such care in how you're holding both your love for your dad and your need to keep living fully. 

What if acceptance isn't about grief winning, but about making space for both your loss and your life to coexist? You don't have to choose between missing him and being present.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Making space for both feels... possible, I guess. But it's still so exhausting to carry all of this every day. I worry that if I stop fighting the pain, I'll just collapse under the weight of it. Maybe accepting it would be easier if I knew how to do that without losing myself completely.
therapist:
You're describing such an understandable fear - that accepting the pain might mean being overwhelmed by it. Yet even through this exhaustion, I hear your determination to find a way through that honors both your grief and your sense of self. 

What comes up for you when you imagine taking small moments of rest with your grief, rather than either fighting it or collapsing under it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
